name: Paul Simon
hook: A New York songwriter who went to Kingston to record reggae in 1971 and to Johannesburg to record with South African musicians in 1985, breaking a UN cultural boycott to make one of the best-selling albums of the decade.

blurb.age13: Paul Simon was born in Newark, New Jersey, in 1941 and grew up in New York. With his school friend Art Garfunkel he formed Simon & Garfunkel, whose last album, 'Bridge over Troubled Water' (1970), is one of the best-selling albums ever. Alone, he went to Kingston, Jamaica, in 1971 to record 'Mother and Child Reunion' with Jamaican musicians, at a time when almost no one outside Jamaica made reggae. In 1985 he went to Johannesburg to record with South African musicians for 'Graceland' (1986). South Africa was then ruled by apartheid, a system that kept Black people separate and without rights by law, and the United Nations had asked artists not to work there. The African National Congress, the main movement fighting apartheid, protested against him. The South African musicians' union had voted to let the sessions go ahead, and Simon paid the players about three times what top New York session players earned. People still argue about whether he was right.
blurb.adult: Born in Newark in 1941 and raised in Queens. Simon & Garfunkel recorded from 1964 to 1970, their later albums co-produced with the engineer Roy Halee, and ended with 'Bridge over Troubled Water' (1970), among the best-selling albums ever made. Solo, he recorded 'Mother and Child Reunion' at Dynamic Sounds in Kingston in 1971 with Jamaican session players including Hux Brown, Jackie Jackson and Winston Grennan, because Jimmy Cliff had recorded 'Vietnam' there; the single was one of the few records by a non-Jamaican to use reggae so prominently when it reached the US and UK top five in 1972. 'Graceland' (August 1986) began with a bootleg cassette of South African mbaqanga lent to him by the musician Heidi Berg, and its core was recorded at Ovation Studios, Johannesburg, in February 1985 with Ray Phiri, Bakithi Kumalo, Ladysmith Black Mambazo and others. The trip broke the UN cultural boycott of apartheid South Africa. The ANC protested and Artists United Against Apartheid criticised him; the South African Black musicians' union had voted to allow the sessions, he paid around triple New York top rates, he was put on the UN blacklist and taken off it in January 1987, and the UN Anti-Apartheid Committee later supported the album. Whether the record was solidarity or a breach of a boycott its targets had asked for is still argued, and Los Lobos have said they were not credited for a track the band says it wrote, which Simon disputes. He retired from touring in 2018 but has gone on releasing records.

signatureTracks.title: Mother and Child Reunion
signatureTracks.whyThisOne: Recorded in Kingston with Jamaican session players: an American pop hit built on a reggae rhythm section.

signatureTracks.title: You Can Call Me Al
signatureTracks.whyThisOne: The biggest single from 'Graceland', with Bakithi Kumalo's South African bass playing at the front of an American pop record.

signatureTracks.title: Homeless
signatureTracks.whyThisOne: Written with Joseph Shabalala of Ladysmith Black Mambazo to a traditional Zulu wedding melody, and sung almost entirely by the group.
